en: The Sūtra on the Observance of the Rainy Season Retreat, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At Jīvakambavana, he observed the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones!..."
O Bhikkhus who have completed the *vassa*, you should speak [to them], you should instruct them, you should admonish them, and you should cherish them, for they are foremost.
For what reason?
Venerable friends!

There may be someone who is perverse, difficult to instruct, and associated with unwholesome qualities; such that even toward those living the holy life (brahmacarya), he neither speaks, nor teaches, nor exhorts, nor shows affection, regarding them as being inferior to himself.
In what way, friends,
is one perverse and difficult to instruct?
It is when those who practice the holy life together with him neither speak to him, nor teach him, nor admonish him, nor show him affection, because he considers himself to be foremost.
"Venerable friends!
There may be a certain person who seeks what is evil and dwells together with those who seek what is evil.
Venerable friends!"

That is to say, such a person seeks what is evil and associates with those who seek what is evil; these qualities are perverse and difficult to instruct. Likewise, they are possessed by defiled desire, hatred, and stinginess; they do not abandon flattery, deceit, and illusion; they lack shame and dread of blame; they are bound by anger and harbor anger in their speech.

Having spoken, he returns with a counter-report; having spoken, he proclaims it to many people; having spoken, he slanders it; each having their own version, they speak it abroad; harboring resentment and fetters, they associate extensively with evil associates and evil companions; they do not recognize kindness or gratitude, nor do they acknowledge past favors.
"Venerable friends!
One who does not recognize kindness and lacks gratitude is perverse and difficult to instruct; this, venerable friends, is what is meant by being perverse and difficult to instruct."

"Regarding those who practice the holy life together with him, he neither speaks to them, nor instructs them, nor admonishes them, nor regards them with affection, because he considers himself to be foremost."
"Venerable friends!
A bhikkhu should reflect within himself.
Venerable friends!"
That person who pursues what is evil and dwells together with what is evil is not respected by me;
if I were to pursue what is evil and dwell together with what is evil, others likewise would not respect me.
A bhikṣu should practice equanimous contemplation; he must not seek through malice, but should train himself thus.

Likewise regarding lustful attachment, hatred, resentment, stinginess, envy, the failure to abandon flattery and deceit, the lack of shame and lack of dread of blame, and the fetters of anger, as well as the verbal expression of the fetters of anger.

Having spoken, a bhikṣu reports back what was said; having spoken, he proclaims it to many people; having spoken, he slanders it; each speaking their own version, they proclaim it abroad; out of resentment, they associate extensively with evil associates and evil companions; they do not recognize kindness, nor do they know how to repay it.
"Virtuous ones!
One who is ungrateful and lacks reciprocity is someone I do not love;
if I were ungrateful and lacked reciprocity, others would likewise not hold me in high regard."
“Monks, you should observe with equanimity; you should not be ungrateful; you should train yourselves like the virtuous.
If a monk has not yet completed his *varṣa* (the rains retreat), you should speak to him, you should instruct him, you should admonish him, and you should cherish him, regarding him as foremost.”
Why is this? Venerable friends!

There may be a person who is not perverse and is in accord with the teaching—meaning one who is in accord with the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Such a person should be spoken to, instructed, and admonished with affection, for that person is considered foremost.
How is it, venerable sirs,
that one is not contrary to the teaching?
It is said that for one who practices the holy life together with others, one should speak for them, instruct them, and admonish them with affection, regarding them as foremost.
"Venerable friends!
There may be a certain person who has no evil desires and does not dwell together with evil desires.
That is to say, venerable friends!"

That person has no evil desires and does not associate with those who have evil desires; this dharma is free from perversity. Thus, they are unstained by desire, free from ill will, and without stinginess or envy; they are without flattery, deceit, or illusion, and are neither shameless nor lacking in moral dread, nor are they bound by the fetter of anger, nor do they speak words of anger.

When a bhikṣu has spoken, he does not fail to give a reply; when a bhikṣu has spoken, he does not fail to speak of it to many people; when a bhikṣu has spoken, he does not slander it. Each has their own discourse which they do not keep secret, nor do they spread it out of malice or resentment. They do not associate with evil friends or evil companions; they are not ungrateful, nor do they act with ingratitude.
"Venerable friends!
When a person is in accord with the teaching, this is what is meant by being 'not contrary' to the teaching.
One who is in accord with the holy life (brahmacariya) should be spoken to, instructed, and admonished with affection, for that person is foremost."
"Venerable friends!
A bhikkhu should reflect within himself.
Venerable friends!"
That person has no evil desires and does not associate with those who have evil desires—this is what I keep in mind;
if I myself have no evil desires and do not associate with those who have evil desires, others will likewise think of me.
A bhikṣu should practice equanimous contemplation; he should not seek through malice, but should train himself thus.

In this way, he is unstained by desire, free from ill will, and without stinginess or envy; he does not abandon [virtue], nor is he flattering, deceitful, or delusive; he is neither shameless nor lacking in moral dread; he is without the fetter of anger, and his mouth utters no words of anger.

When a bhikṣu has spoken, he does not fail to respond; when a bhikṣu has spoken, he does not fail to speak of it to many people; when a bhikṣu has spoken, he does not disparage it. Each person speaks according to what they have been taught without broadcasting it abroad; they do not spread it out of anger or resentment. They do not associate with evil friends or evil companions, nor are they ungrateful or unreciprocating.
"Venerable friends!
That person who is not ungrateful and not unreciprocating is one whom I hold dear;

if I am not ungrateful and not unreciprocating, others will also hold me dear. My bhikkhus should practice equanimity toward those who are not ungrateful and not unreciprocating, and you should train yourselves in this way."
"Venerable friends!
When a bhikkhu has reflected thus, it is of great benefit: 'I am dwelling with evil seeking and accompanied by evil seeking; shall I not dwell with evil seeking and accompanied by evil seeking?'"
When these venerable bhikkhus observe and know: "I dwell in evil seeking and am associated with evil seeking," they will not take delight in it;
they will then advance with the desire to bring it to rest.
"Venerable friends!

A bhikkhu observes and knows: 'I shall not dwell with evil seeking, nor be accompanied by evil seeking. He then rejoices in that purity and clarity, which is the sphere of practice of the Buddha, the World-Honored One; having seen it, he delights in practicing it."
It is just as if, worthy ones,
a man with sight were to take an extremely clean mirror and use it to observe his own face. This,
worthy ones, is how it is.
A person with eyes, seeing the dust and grime upon their own face, does not take pleasure in it; they instead strive to remove that impurity.
Venerable friends!
A person with eyes, not seeing dust and grime upon their own face, takes delight in its purity and, having seen this, finds joy in practicing accordingly.
In this way, worthy friends, a bhikkhu observes and knows:
"I am dwelling with evil pursuits and accompanied by evil pursuits; let me exert myself to bring them to rest.
This, worthy friends, is so.

The bhikṣu observes and knows: "I shall not abide in evil seeking nor associate with evil seeking. He then becomes joyful, pure, and bright, dwelling within the domain of the Buddha, the World-Honored One; having seen this, he delights in its practice.
Thus they dwell in lustful desire, not dwelling in the absence of lustful desire; thus they dwell in anger and resentment, not dwelling in the absence of anger and resentment;
thus they dwell in stinginess, envy, and non-renunciation, not dwelling in the absence of stinginess, envy, and non-renunciation;
thus they dwell in flattery, deceit, and illusion, not dwelling in the absence of flattery, deceit, and illusion; thus they dwell in shamelessness and...
Shame is neither non-abiding nor non-lack-of-shame nor non-lack-of-bashfulness;

thus one abides in the fetter of ill-will while speaking words of ill-will, yet does not abide in the fetter of ill-will while speaking words of ill-will. When a bhikṣu speaks, he returns that speech;
he does not fail to return the speech when a bhikṣu has spoken. When a bhikṣu speaks, he reports it to many people... [does not...]
When a bhikṣu has spoken, one does not repeat his words to many people; when a bhikṣu has spoken, one does not speak with derision;
when a bhikṣu has spoken, one does not fail to speak with derision; each speaks according to what they have said, yet one does not speak it out to others;
one harbors resentment, yet one does not fail to harbor resentment. And...
He frequently associates with evil friends and evil companions; he does not abide in non-association with evil friends or evil companions.
He is ungrateful and fails to repay kindness; he does not abide in being neither ungrateful nor failing to repay kindness.
"Venerable friends!
When a bhikkhu observes and knows: 'I dwell without gratitude and without requital,' he becomes displeased and strives to bring that state to an end."
"Venerable friends!

When a bhikkhu observes and knows: 'I dwell without ingratitude and I dwell with gratitude,' he then becomes joyful, pure, and bright; he practices within the sphere of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and having seen this for himself, he delights in that practice."
It is just as if, worthy ones,
a man with sight were to take a clear mirror and look at his own face. This,
worthy ones, is the case.
When a person with sight sees dust and grime upon their own face, they become displeased and seek to remove it.
Venerable friends, when such a person with sight does not see dust and grime upon their own face, they rejoice in their purity; having seen this for themselves, they delight in practicing it.
In this way, worthy friends!
A bhikkhu observes and knows; dwelling without gratitude or reciprocity, he does not find joy and thus immediately advances toward cessation.
This, worthy friends!

The bhikṣu observes and knows: "While I abide, I am not without gratitude and reciprocity; he [the Buddha] is thus joyful, pure, and bright, practicing within the sphere of the Buddha, the World-Honored One."

Having seen for oneself, one practices with joy; having practiced with joy, one experiences gladness; having experienced gladness, the body experiences faith and practice; having the body experience faith and practice, one knows peace and happiness; having peace and happiness, the mind becomes concentrated; with a concentrated mind, one knows things as they truly are and sees them as they truly are; having known and seen things as they truly are, one is without weariness; being without weariness, one is without defilement; being without defilement, one is liberated; having been liberated, one attains the knowledge of liberation, knowing as it truly is: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
Thus spoke the venerable Maudgalyāyana. Having heard what the venerable Maudgalyāyana had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and were delighted.

Regarding this Sūtra on Observing the *Varṣā* (the Rain Retreat) spoken by the Buddha: in the Danzang edition it is titled "Sūtra on Observing the *Varṣā*," which exists in the Dan edition but not in the Song edition;
in the Songzang edition it is titled "Sūtra on Observing the New Year," which exists in the Song edition but not in the Dan edition.

According to both scriptures, they were translated by Dharmarakṣa; yet while their titles are slightly similar, their meanings differ greatly. Thus, it remains unknown which is correct and which is erroneous, and furthermore, why there are mutual discrepancies regarding their inclusion or exclusion from the Two Tripitakas.

Now, examining the *Kaiyuan lu*, within the section on "Re-translations" (Chóngyì lù) under the category of the Rong (容) case, there is the *Shòusuì jīng* (Sūtra on Receiving the Year), translated by Zhu Fahu. It states that this is a different translation of the same original text as the beginning of the twenty-third fascicle of the *Zhōngāhán jīng*. Furthermore, within the section on "Single Translations" (Dānyì lù) under the category of the Jìng (竟) case, there is the *Xīnsuì jīng* (New Sūtra on the Year), translated by Zhu Tanwulan (whose name was rendered as Fǎzhèng in Chinese).
A note therein states: "The major version of the *Zhōngāhán* does not contain these sūtras; therefore, they have been compiled here."

Now, upon examining the *Dan shousui jing* (Sanskrit: *Varṣā-śrāmaṇera-sūtra*), it is largely identical to the twenty-third fascicle of that *Madhyama Āgama*; thus, it is truly a retranslation of the *Shousui jing* by Dharmarakṣa.

The *Sòngběn shòu xīnsuì jīng* (New Year Sūtra from the Song Edition) is entirely different from that [version] in the *Madhyama Āgama*; however, as for the *Xīnsuì jīng* found in the Jìng box, although the wording differs, the general purport is no different, and it appears to be an alternative translation of that same sūtra.

However, regarding this "Sūtra on Welcoming the New Year" in the present *Rong* (容) fascicle of the Song Canon and that "Sūtra on Welcoming the New Year" in the *Jing* (竟) fascicle, if they were considered single translations, how could there be such differences in length—extensive versus abbreviated—and discrepancies in the translators? Furthermore, why would this [present version] be included among the "re-translations"?
If one considers this to be a "re-translated" (zhòngyì) version, then why is it listed among the "single-translated" (dānyì) texts?
This must await further verification.

For now, wishing to categorize them for the sake of future scholars and sages, I have moved the *Shòu xīnsuì jīng* (Sūtra on Receiving the New Year) into the final fascicle; from within this volume, one may take this [text] from the Danzang as the authentic copy.
